title: Maximum Subarray Min-Product
description: Brute force to optimized: tracking min and sum incrementally for every starting index versus a monotonic stack for each index's widest span as the minimum, combined with prefix sums.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: The min-product of an array is the minimum value in the array, multiplied by the sum of the array. Given an integer array nums (all values positive), find the maximum min-product of any non-empty contiguous subarray of nums. Return the answer modulo 1,000,000,007.

blocks.text: For every possible non-empty contiguous subarray, multiply its minimum element by its total sum. Find the largest such product across all subarrays.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Best Trade-off Between a Weak Link and Total Volume
blocks.text: Picture a subarray as a chain, its "strength" being its weakest link (the minimum), multiplied by its total "volume" (the sum). A longer chain has more volume, but adding more links can only lower or maintain the weakest link, so the best chain balances length against not diluting its weakest link too much.

blocks.caption: For each index, its widest span where it remains the minimum, bounded by nearer smaller elements

blocks.text: The subarray [2,3,2] has minimum 2 and sum 7, giving a min-product of 14, the best possible.
The subarray [3,3] has minimum 3 and sum 6, giving a min-product of 18.
The subarray [5,6,4] has minimum 4 and sum 15, giving a min-product of 60.
Before checking every subarray's minimum and sum directly, notice that for any fixed index treated as "the minimum," there is a well-defined widest subarray where it actually remains the minimum.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For index i to be the minimum of a subarray, that subarray cannot extend past the nearest element to the left, or to the right, that is smaller than nums[i].

Observation 2: The widest possible subarray where nums[i] is the minimum spans exactly from just after its nearest smaller element on the left, to just before its nearest smaller element on the right.

Observation 3: Since a larger sum only helps the min-product (values are positive), the best candidate for index i as the minimum is always this single widest span, no other width for this same minimum needs checking.

Observation 4: The nearest smaller element to the left and right, for every index, can be found in O(n) total using a monotonic increasing stack, and the span's sum can be found in O(1) with a prefix sum array.

This leads directly to: for every index, use a monotonic stack to find its nearest smaller neighbors on both sides, then use prefix sums to get that widest span's sum in O(1), and take the best min-product across all indices.
For every possible subarray, track its minimum and its sum directly as it grows, and compute the min-product at each step.

items: For every starting index i, extend an ending index j from i onward.
Maintain the running minimum and running sum of nums[i..j] incrementally.
At each j, compute the running minimum times the running sum, and track the best value seen.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: track min and sum incrementally for every starting index

codes.python:
def max_sum_min_product(nums):
    MOD = 1_000_000_007
    n = len(nums)
    best = 0
    for i in range(n):
        cur_min, cur_sum = nums[i], 0
        for j in range(i, n):
            cur_min = min(cur_min, nums[j])       # widen the subarray, recheck the minimum
            cur_sum += nums[j]
            best = max(best, cur_min * cur_sum)
    return best % MOD

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The running minimum and running sum are both updated incrementally as j grows, avoiding a full rescan of the subarray at each step.
Every starting index i is still tried independently, giving O(n squared) total pairs even though each individual update is O(1).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), every pair of start and end indices is examined, even with O(1) incremental updates per step.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: for a fixed starting index, extending further right can only ever lower or maintain the running minimum, meaning most of these n squared candidates are dominated by a single best choice per minimum value, one that can be found directly instead of through this exhaustive scan.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why scanning every start and end pair is wasteful: for a specific value acting as the minimum, the best possible subarray using it is always its single WIDEST valid span, since sum only grows as the span widens and the minimum cannot improve.

What defines that widest valid span for index i: it extends exactly from just after the nearest smaller element to the left, to just before the nearest smaller element to the right, since going further in either direction would include a smaller value, changing the minimum.

How to find those nearest smaller neighbors efficiently: a monotonic increasing stack processed left to right (for nearest smaller to the left) and right to left (for nearest smaller to the right), each in O(n) total.

How to get that span's sum quickly: a prefix sum array, giving any range's sum in O(1).

The core idea: for every index, find its widest span as the minimum using two monotonic stack passes, look up that span's sum with prefix sums, and take the best min-product across all indices.

Build a prefix sum array. Using a monotonic increasing stack, find the nearest strictly smaller element to the left and to the right of every index. For each index, its widest valid span as the minimum runs from just after its left neighbor to just before its right neighbor; look up that span's sum in O(1) and multiply by nums[i], tracking the best result.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: monotonic stack for the widest span, prefix sums for its total

codes.python:
def max_sum_min_product(nums):
    MOD = 1_000_000_007
    n = len(nums)
    prefix = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(n):
        prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]

    left_smaller = [-1] * n
    stack = []
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] >= nums[i]:
            stack.pop()
        left_smaller[i] = stack[-1] if stack else -1        # nearest strictly smaller, to the left
        stack.append(i)

    right_smaller = [n] * n
    stack = []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] >= nums[i]:
            stack.pop()
        right_smaller[i] = stack[-1] if stack else n         # nearest strictly smaller, to the right
        stack.append(i)

    best = 0
    for i in range(n):
        span_sum = prefix[right_smaller[i]] - prefix[left_smaller[i] + 1]  # widest span's sum, O(1)
        best = max(best, nums[i] * span_sum)
    return best % MOD

blocks.text: For any index used as the minimum, the widest span in which it remains the minimum is bounded exactly by its nearest strictly smaller neighbors, going any further would introduce a smaller value. Since every value is positive, a wider span always has a larger or equal sum, so this single widest span is always at least as good as any narrower one using the same minimum, making it the only candidate that needs checking per index.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), two monotonic stack passes plus one pass to compute the answer, each index pushed and popped at most once per pass.
Space: O(n) for the prefix sums, the stacks, and the nearest-smaller arrays.

blocks.text: The key insight is that for any value acting as a subarray's minimum, only its single widest valid span ever needs to be checked, since extending as far as possible without introducing a smaller value always maximizes the sum for that minimum. This turns an O(n squared) search into an O(n) one using the classic monotonic-stack "nearest smaller element" technique paired with prefix sums.

items: Checking multiple widths for the same minimum value instead of realizing only the single widest span ever matters.
Using a non-strict comparison in the monotonic stack, which can cause equal values to be double-counted or spans to be computed incorrectly.
Forgetting to apply the modulo only at the very end, after computing the true (potentially very large) product.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single-element array","The min-product is simply that element squared."],["All elements equal","The whole array is the best subarray, its minimum times its full sum."]]}

blocks.text: Explaining why extending a subarray past the nearest smaller neighbor can only hurt (introducing a smaller minimum) while never being required to help (sum was already maximized within the valid range) is the key justification for why only one span per index needs checking.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how do you avoid checking every possible width for each minimum", think: only the widest span before a smaller element interrupts it ever needs to be considered.
If the interviewer says "how do you find that widest span efficiently", think: a monotonic increasing stack, run once left to right and once right to left.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time and O(1) space. The optimized monotonic-stack-plus-prefix-sum approach runs in O(n) time and O(n) space.

items: Pattern: monotonic stack for nearest-smaller-element spans, combined with prefix sums for O(1) range sums.
Core Idea: for each index as the minimum, only its single widest valid span (bounded by nearer smaller elements) ever needs to be checked.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: since all values are positive, the widest span for a given minimum always has the largest possible sum for that minimum, so no narrower span needs checking.
Interview Difficulty: requires recognizing the monotonic-stack span technique; a common and reusable idea once seen.
One line memory trick: for each index, find its widest span as the minimum with a monotonic stack, then multiply by that span's prefix sum.
